difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE because the single concept involved (rank/nullity conditions for existence and uniqueness of solutions of Mx = b) is applied directly, which alone would be EASY, but each of the four statements needs its own construction or impossibility argument, which moves the MSQ up one level; about two minutes for a prepared student.
stem:
Which of the following statements is/are **TRUE**?

**Note:** $\mathbb{R}$ denotes the set of real numbers.

options.label: A
options.text: There exist $\boldsymbol{M} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, \boldsymbol{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3,$ and $\boldsymbol{q} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ such that $\boldsymbol{M}\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{p}$ has a unique solution and $\boldsymbol{M}\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{q}$ has infinite solutions.

options.label: B
options.text: There exist $\boldsymbol{M} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, \boldsymbol{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3,$ and $\boldsymbol{q} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ such that $\boldsymbol{M}\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{p}$ has no solutions and $\boldsymbol{M}\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{q}$ has infinite solutions.

options.label: C
options.text: There exist $\boldsymbol{M} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3}, \boldsymbol{p} \in \mathbb{R}^2,$ and $\boldsymbol{q} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ such that $\boldsymbol{M}\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{p}$ has a unique solution and $\boldsymbol{M}\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{q}$ has infinite solutions.

options.label: D
options.text: There exist $\boldsymbol{M} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 2}, \boldsymbol{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3,$ and $\boldsymbol{q} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ such that $\boldsymbol{M}\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{p}$ has a unique solution and $\boldsymbol{M}\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{q}$ has no solutions.

solution.quick: Whether $\boldsymbol{M}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has *a* solution depends on $\mathbf{b}$ (is $\mathbf{b}$ in the column space?), but whether a solution, once it exists, is *unique* depends only on $\boldsymbol{M}$ (is $\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{M}$ equal to the number of columns?). So "unique" and "infinite" can never occur for the same $\boldsymbol{M}$: (A) is false, and (C) is false because a $2 \times 3$ matrix has rank $\le 2 < 3$. A singular $3 \times 3$ matrix gives "none" and "infinite" (B), and a rank-2 $3 \times 2$ matrix gives "unique" and "none" (D). Answer: **(B), (D)**.

steps.title: The rule that decides the number of solutions
steps.body:
For $\boldsymbol{M} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ (so $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$) and a right-hand side $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^m$, the Rouché–Capelli (rank) test says:

- **no solution** if $\operatorname{rank}[\boldsymbol{M} \mid \mathbf{b}] > \operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{M}$, i.e. $\mathbf{b}$ is not in the column space $C(\boldsymbol{M})$;
- **exactly one solution** if $\operatorname{rank}[\boldsymbol{M} \mid \mathbf{b}] = \operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{M} = n$;
- **infinitely many solutions** if $\operatorname{rank}[\boldsymbol{M} \mid \mathbf{b}] = \operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{M} < n$.

The reason: if $\mathbf{x}_0$ is one solution, the full solution set is $\mathbf{x}_0 + N(\boldsymbol{M})$, where $N(\boldsymbol{M})$ is the null space. That set is a single point when the nullity $n - \operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{M}$ is $0$ and infinite otherwise. **Uniqueness is a property of $\boldsymbol{M}$ alone**; only the question "is there any solution?" depends on the right-hand side.

For a fixed $\boldsymbol{M}$ with rank $r$, over all possible right-hand sides:

| Behaviour | Possible for some right-hand side iff |
| --- | --- |
| no solution | $r < m$ (column space is not all of $\mathbb{R}^m$) |
| unique solution | $r = n$ (null space is $\{\mathbf{0}\}$) |
| infinitely many solutions | $r < n$ (e.g. take $\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0}$) |

"Unique" needs $r = n$ and "infinite" needs $r < n$, so these two can never both happen for the same $\boldsymbol{M}$.

steps.title: (A) Square, unique and infinite: impossible
steps.body: If $\boldsymbol{M}\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{p}$ has a unique solution, the nullity of $\boldsymbol{M}$ is $0$, so $\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{M} = 3$ and the $3 \times 3$ matrix $\boldsymbol{M}$ is invertible. Then for **every** $\boldsymbol{q} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ the system $\boldsymbol{M}\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{q}$ has exactly one solution, $\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{M}^{-1}\boldsymbol{q}$. It can never have infinitely many. (A) is **false**.

steps.title: (B) Square singular matrix: none and infinite, true
steps.body:
Any singular $\boldsymbol{M}$ ($\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{M} \le 2$) works. Take

$$
\boldsymbol{M} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \boldsymbol{p} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \boldsymbol{q} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

- $\boldsymbol{M}\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{p}$: the third equation reads $0 \cdot x_1 + 0 \cdot x_2 + 0 \cdot x_3 = 1$, i.e. $0 = 1$, so there is **no solution** ($\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{M} = 2$, $\operatorname{rank}[\boldsymbol{M} \mid \boldsymbol{p}] = 3$).
- $\boldsymbol{M}\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{q}$: the equations are $x_1 = 0$, $x_2 = 0$, $0 = 0$, so every $\mathbf{x} = (0, 0, t)^\top$, $t \in \mathbb{R}$, is a solution: **infinitely many** ($\operatorname{rank} = 2 < 3$).

(B) is **true**.

steps.title: (C) Wide 2 × 3 matrix: never unique
steps.body: A $2 \times 3$ matrix has $\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{M} \le 2$ (only two rows), while there are $n = 3$ unknowns. By rank–nullity, the nullity is $3 - \operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{M} \ge 1$, so $N(\boldsymbol{M})$ contains a non-zero vector $\mathbf{v}$. Whenever $\boldsymbol{M}\mathbf{x}_0 = \boldsymbol{p}$, every $\mathbf{x}_0 + t\mathbf{v}$ is also a solution. Two equations in three unknowns therefore have either no solution or infinitely many, **never exactly one**. The first half of (C) is impossible, so (C) is **false** (even though $\boldsymbol{M}\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{q}$ having infinitely many solutions is easy to arrange).

steps.title: (D) Tall 3 × 2 matrix of rank 2: unique and none, true
steps.body:
Take a $3 \times 2$ matrix with independent columns, e.g.

$$
\boldsymbol{M} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \boldsymbol{p} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \boldsymbol{q} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

- $\boldsymbol{M}\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{p}$: the equations are $x_1 = 1$, $x_2 = 2$, $0 = 0$, so $\mathbf{x} = (1, 2)^\top$ is the **unique** solution ($\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{M} = \operatorname{rank}[\boldsymbol{M} \mid \boldsymbol{p}] = 2 = n$).
- $\boldsymbol{M}\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{q}$: the third equation reads $0 = 1$, so there is **no solution** ($\operatorname{rank}[\boldsymbol{M} \mid \boldsymbol{q}] = 3 > 2$).

Geometrically, $C(\boldsymbol{M})$ is a plane in $\mathbb{R}^3$: a right-hand side on the plane gives exactly one solution, and one off the plane gives none. (D) is **true**.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: (A) needs the same $\boldsymbol{M}$ to have nullity $0$ and nullity $> 0$, and (C) needs a $2 \times 3$ system to have a unique solution; both are impossible. (B) (singular square matrix) and (D) (tall matrix with full column rank) are realised by the explicit examples above. The answer is **(B), (D)**.

solution.teaching:
**Two separate questions hide inside "how many solutions?".** For a linear system $\boldsymbol{M}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ with $\boldsymbol{M}$ of size $m \times n$, ask:

1. **Is there any solution?** $\boldsymbol{M}\mathbf{x}$ is a linear combination of the columns of $\boldsymbol{M}$, so a solution exists exactly when $\mathbf{b}$ lies in the column space $C(\boldsymbol{M})$. This depends on $\mathbf{b}$. If $\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{M} = m$, the columns fill $\mathbb{R}^m$ and every $\mathbf{b}$ works; if $\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{M} < m$, some $\mathbf{b}$ fail.
2. **If so, how many?** If $\mathbf{x}_0$ solves the system, so does $\mathbf{x}_0 + \mathbf{v}$ for every $\mathbf{v}$ in the null space $N(\boldsymbol{M})$, and every solution has this form. So the count is $1$ when $N(\boldsymbol{M}) = \{\mathbf{0}\}$ (rank $= n$) and infinite otherwise. This depends **only on $\boldsymbol{M}$**.

A linear system therefore never has "exactly two" solutions, and one matrix can never give a unique solution for one right-hand side and infinitely many for another.

**The shape of $\boldsymbol{M}$ tells you what is possible:**

| Shape and rank | Possible outcomes |
| --- | --- |
| square, invertible | always unique |
| square, singular | none or infinite |
| wide ($m < n$) | infinite for every right-hand side if rank $= m$; none or infinite if rank $< m$; never unique |
| tall ($m > n$), rank $n$ | unique or none |
| tall, rank $< n$ | none or infinite |

**Back to this question.** (A) asks a square matrix for "unique" and "infinite" together, which would need nullity $0$ and nullity $> 0$ at once. (C) asks a wide $2 \times 3$ matrix for a unique solution, but its null space is at least one-dimensional. (B) is the square singular row of the table, for example $\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, 0)$ with $\boldsymbol{p} = (0, 0, 1)^\top$ and $\boldsymbol{q} = \mathbf{0}$. (D) is the tall, full-column-rank row: the column space is a plane in $\mathbb{R}^3$, so points on it give one solution and points off it give none. Answer: **(B), (D)**.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: A unique solution of $\boldsymbol{M}\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{p}$ forces nullity $0$, i.e. $\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{M} = 3$, so the $3 \times 3$ matrix is invertible and $\boldsymbol{M}\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{q}$ has the unique solution $\boldsymbol{M}^{-1}\boldsymbol{q}$ for every $\boldsymbol{q}$. Infinitely many solutions are impossible.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Any singular $\boldsymbol{M}$ works. With $\boldsymbol{M} = \operatorname{diag}(1, 1, 0)$: $\boldsymbol{p} = (0, 0, 1)^\top$ gives the equation $0 = 1$ (no solution), and $\boldsymbol{q} = \mathbf{0}$ gives $\mathbf{x} = (0, 0, t)^\top$ for all $t$ (infinitely many).

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: A $2 \times 3$ matrix has rank at most $2 < 3$ unknowns, so its null space is non-trivial and any consistent system $\boldsymbol{M}\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{p}$ has infinitely many solutions. A unique solution is impossible.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: With $\boldsymbol{M} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ (rank 2): $\boldsymbol{p} = (1, 2, 0)^\top$ gives the unique solution $\mathbf{x} = (1, 2)^\top$, and $\boldsymbol{q} = (0, 0, 1)^\top$ lies outside the column space, so it gives no solution.

solution.shortcut: "Unique vs infinite" is decided by $\boldsymbol{M}$ alone (nullity $0$ or not), so any statement pairing *unique* with *infinite* for the same $\boldsymbol{M}$ is false: that removes (A) and (C) (and (C) already fails because a wide matrix can never give a unique solution). "No solution" pairs with either of the others as long as $\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{M} <$ number of rows, which a singular $3 \times 3$ (B) and a rank-2 $3 \times 2$ (D) both satisfy.
solution.commonTrap: Believing that for the same square matrix one right-hand side can give a unique solution and another infinitely many, and so marking (A). The number of solutions of a consistent system is fixed by the null space of $\boldsymbol{M}$, not by the right-hand side. A second trap is rejecting (D) because a $3 \times 2$ system is "overdetermined": it has a unique solution whenever $\boldsymbol{p}$ lies in the column space.

transcription.notes: Transcribed from the official paper rendering and independently checked against it. Stem, note and all four options match the rendering word for word, including the matrix sizes (3×3, 3×3, 2×3, 3×2) and vector spaces (ℝ³, ℝ³, ℝ², ℝ³) in each option. The paper sets M, p and q in bold italic and x in upright bold; these are transcribed as \boldsymbol{M}, \boldsymbol{p}, \boldsymbol{q} and \mathbf{x}. The PDF text layer shows the M in the second equation of each option as a plain 'M', but the rendering shows it in the same bold italic as elsewhere, so \boldsymbol{M} is used throughout. Wording such as 'has infinite solutions' and 'has no solutions' follows the paper.

answerVerification.method: Blind independent re-solve + Python check agrees with official key
answerVerification.checkCode:
import itertools, numpy as np
r=np.linalg.matrix_rank
def count(M,b,rM=None):  # Rouche-Capelli: 0, 1 or 'inf' solutions of Mx=b
    rM=r(M) if rM is None else rM; rA=r(np.column_stack([M,b]))
    return 0 if rA>rM else (1 if rM==M.shape[1] else 'inf')
# Worked examples
M=np.diag([1.,1,0]); print('B:', count(M,[0,0,1]), count(M,[0,0,0]))          # 0 inf -> (B) true
M=np.array([[1.,0],[0,1],[0,0]]); print('D:', count(M,[1,2,0]), count(M,[0,0,1]))  # 1 0 -> (D) true
# Brute force: every M with entries in {-1,0,1}, every rhs b in {-1,0,1}^m, actually solved via ranks
def outcomes(m,n):
    B=[np.array(b,float) for b in itertools.product([-1,0,1],repeat=m)]; out=set()
    for e in itertools.product([-1,0,1],repeat=m*n):
        M=np.array(e,float).reshape(m,n); rM=r(M); out.add(frozenset(count(M,b,rM) for b in B))
    return out
o33,o23,o32=outcomes(3,3),outcomes(2,3),outcomes(3,2)
print('A possible:', any({1,'inf'}<=s for s in o33))   # False
print('B possible:', any({0,'inf'}<=s for s in o33))   # True
print('C possible:', any({1,'inf'}<=s for s in o23))   # False (1 never occurs for 2x3)
print('D possible:', any({1,0}<=s for s in o32))       # True
answerVerification.notes: Blind re-solve (before viewing the key): a unique solution of Mx = p forces nullity 0, so M cannot also give infinitely many solutions for another right-hand side; this rules out (A) (3x3) and (C) (2x3 has rank <= 2 < 3 unknowns, so it can never have a unique solution). A singular 3x3 matrix gives 'none' for p outside its column space and 'infinite' for q inside it (B), and a rank-2 3x2 matrix gives 'unique' for p in its column space (a plane in R^3) and 'none' for q off it (D). Independent answer B;D. The Python check confirms the explicit examples and brute-forces every matrix with entries in {-1,0,1} against every right-hand side in {-1,0,1}^m, finding the outcome pairs of (B) and (D) but never those of (A) or (C). This matches the official key B;D.
